title: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
summary: Why two components read one input differently: double decoding, UTF-8 overlongs, normalisation, case mapping, confusables, bidi Trojan Source and URL, JSON, XML and multipart parser differentials, with fixes.
outcomes: Explain why check-then-transform and two-parser designs produce bypasses, and place each check after the last transformation
Decode UTF-8, percent and base64 strictly and explain overlong forms, double decoding and non-canonical encodings
Apply NFC, NFKC and case folding correctly, and test canonicalisation functions for idempotence
Detect confusables with UTS #39 skeletons and explain how browsers decide to show an IDN as Punycode
Explain how bidi controls make reviewed code differ from compiled code, and block them in CI
Find and fix URL, JSON, XML, multipart and email parser differentials by parsing once and rejecting ambiguity
Use the Spotify, Django, CouchDB, PHP-CGI, ruby-saml and Trojan Source cases to plan detection and response

lessons.title: One input, many readers: where encoding bugs come from

blocks.md:
A request for a file passes through several programs before anything opens the file: maybe a gateway that filters requests, then the web framework, then your code, then the operating system. Each of them **reads** the bytes: it decodes them, splits them into parts, maybe tidies them up. If two of those readers turn the same bytes into different meanings, an attacker gets to choose which meaning each reader sees.

A tiny example. A filter refuses any path containing `..` (the parent-directory step: `a/../b` means `b`; using it to climb out of an allowed folder is called **path traversal**). The request asks for `%2e%2e/etc/passwd`. The filter sees no `..` and lets it through. The application then percent-decodes it, and `%2e` is a dot, so it opens `../etc/passwd`. (Path traversal itself, and safe path joins, are covered in Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling.)

Some words this course uses constantly:

- **Decoding**: turning an encoded form back into the value it stands for, like `%2e` into `.`. You met base64, hex and percent-encoding in Python for security work.
- **Parser**: code that turns text or bytes into structure, such as a URL into scheme, host and path, or JSON into a dictionary.
- **Canonical form**: the one standard spelling chosen for a value that can be written many ways. **Canonicalisation** is converting input into it. Microsoft's 2000 bulletin for an IIS (Internet Information Services, Microsoft's web server) traversal bug calls the root cause "a canonicalization error".
- **Parser differential**: GitHub Security Lab's (GitHub's vulnerability research team) definition is "when different parsers interpret the same input in different ways".

blocks.caption: Output: `ALLOWED /srv/files/report.pdf` / `BLOCKED ../etc/passwd` / `ALLOWED /srv/files/../etc/passwd`

blocks.title: Four readers, three different views of one path

scenes.caption: The raw request path arrives. Every box will read it, but not all of them read it the same way.
The gateway filter looks for `..` in the raw text. `%2e%2e` contains no dot at all, so the check passes.
The application percent-decodes the path. Now the value really is `../etc/passwd`, but nobody checks it again.
The filesystem resolves `..` and steps out of /srv/files. The check ran on one meaning; the action used another.
The fix moves the check to the last reader that changes the meaning: decode, resolve the full path, then check that exact path.

blocks.caption: Output: `ALLOWED /srv/files/report.pdf` / `BLOCKED ../etc/passwd -> outside /srv/files` / `BLOCKED %2e%2e/etc/passwd -> outside /srv/files`. On a real server use `os.path.realpath`, which also follows symbolic links.

blocks.md:
Why the fix works: the check now runs on **the exact value that will be used**, after every step that can change its meaning. `os.path.normpath` resolves `..` the way the filesystem will, and `os.path.commonpath` confirms the result is still under the base folder. However the attacker spells the path, the decision is made on what it finally means.

Two root causes repeat through this whole course:

1. **Check, then transform.** Validation runs before a later step (decoding, normalising, case mapping, character set conversion) changes the data.
2. **One input, two parsers.** Two components each parse the same bytes and act on their own result.

HTTP request smuggling is the second pattern applied to message framing, where a proxy and a server disagree about where one request ends; it has its own course, HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks. Injection, where data turns into code, is taught in Injection: when data becomes code. This course is about the text and structure layers underneath both.

Misconception: "the filter should just decode more". A filter in front of an application cannot know how many decoding or normalising steps come later, or in what order. Make the component that acts on the value own the check, and treat upstream filters as an extra layer, not the defence.

**Defender view.** Prevent: validate after the last transformation, in the component that acts. Detect: log both the raw request line and the decoded value your code used; a large difference between them (encoded dots, encoded slashes, `%25`) is a signal worth alerting on, and so is any request your strict decoder rejects. Respond: when you find a differential, fix the code path and then search past logs for raw values whose decoded form would have crossed the boundary.
Check the value you will use, in the form you will use it, after every step that can change its meaning. Anything else is checking a different string.

blocks.question: A gateway blocks paths containing `..`; the app behind it percent-decodes the path and opens the file. Which change actually closes the hole?
options: Make the gateway also block the string `%2e%2e`
Lower-case the path in the gateway before checking
In the app, decode, resolve the full path and check it is inside the base folder before opening
Return a generic error page so attackers learn less
blocks.explain: Blocking one encoded spelling leaves the others (`%2E%2e`, double encoding, and more). Resolving and checking the final path in the component that opens the file covers every spelling, because the decision is made on what the path finally means.

blocks.question: Which situation is a parser differential?
options: A proxy and the server behind it decide differently where an HTTP request ends
A function crashes on an empty string
One library is slower than another at parsing JSON
A parser rejects input that breaks the specification
blocks.explain: A differential is two parsers reaching different results from the same input. Speed, crashes on edge cases and strict rejection are not disagreements between two readers.

lessons.title: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack

blocks.md:
An attacker loves a value that can be written more than one way. If your check matches one spelling and a later decoder accepts another, the check is decoration. This lesson looks at two encodings you already use, UTF-8 and base64, and the spare room inside each that lazy decoders let through.

Recall from Python for security work: UTF-8 turns each Unicode code point into 1 to 4 bytes. The bit patterns are fixed by [RFC 3629](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629.txt):

- U+0000 to U+007F: `0xxxxxxx` (7 payload bits)
- U+0080 to U+07FF: `110xxxxx 10xxxxxx` (11 bits)
- U+0800 to U+FFFF: `1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` (16 bits)
- U+10000 to U+10FFFF: `11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` (21 bits)

The leading bits of the first byte say how many bytes follow; every continuation byte starts with `10`.

Nothing in those patterns physically stops you from putting a small number into a big box. A dot is U+002E. Its correct encoding is the single byte `2E`. But the two-byte pattern has 11 payload bits, and 00000101110 is still 0x2E, so `110 00000` `10 101110`, the bytes `C0 AE`, would also mean "dot" to a decoder that only does the arithmetic. That is an **overlong encoding**: a longer-than-necessary form of a code point.

RFC 3629 makes overlongs illegal and warns about exactly this: a parser might block `2F 2E 2E 2F` (`/../`) yet accept `2F C0 AE 2E 2F`, and the RFC notes that this "has actually been used in a widespread virus attacking Web servers in 2001".

blocks.title: A dot in one byte, and the same dot in an illegal two-byte box

scenes.caption: The dot U+002E in binary. Its correct UTF-8 form is one byte, 0x2E, pattern 0xxxxxxx.
A two-byte sequence carries 11 payload bits: 5 in the first byte after 110, 6 in the second after 10. The dot's 11-bit value fits.
Filling the box gives C0 AE. A decoder that just shifts and adds bits gets 0x2E back: a dot no byte-level check for 2E ever saw.
A conforming decoder rejects it: any lead byte C0 or C1 can only start an overlong, so RFC 3629 bans those bytes outright. Python's strict decoder raises an error.

blocks.caption: Output: `False` / `'/../'` / `strict: invalid start byte` / `2e c3a9`. The toy decoder is deliberately wrong; Python's real one is strict.

blocks.md: **Case: IIS, 2000.** Microsoft's bulletin [MS00-078](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2000/ms00-078) (17 October 2000, CVE-2000-0884, "Web Server Folder Traversal") describes a canonicalization error in IIS 4.0 and 5.0: a malformed URL could reach files anywhere on the drive holding the web folders. NVD's record says the URLs "contain UNICODE encoded characters". Requests ran as `IUSR_machinename`, the anonymous web account, which by default could run most operating system commands. The patch, the bulletin says, "eliminates the vulnerability by treating the malformed URL as invalid". That sentence is the whole defence for this lesson: reject, never repair.

Base64 has spare room too. It packs 6 bits per character, so one byte (8 bits) of input needs two characters (12 bits), and 4 of those bits are padding. [RFC 4648](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4648.txt) section 3.5 says encoders must set those **pad bits** to zero, and that otherwise "multiple base-encoded strings can be decoded to the same binary data"; decoders "MAY" reject non-zero pad bits. Section 3.3 adds that non-alphabet characters inside encoded data can be a covert channel.

Why it matters: if a system blocks or deduplicates by the encoded text (a list of known-bad tokens, a cache key, a signature over the string) but acts on the decoded bytes, two spellings of the same bytes split the decision from the action.

blocks.caption: Output: `b'fo' b'fo'` / `b'fo'` / `validate=True: Only base64 data is allowed` / `Zm8= b'fo'` / `Zm9= non-canonical base64`

blocks.md: Read the output: `Zm8=` and `Zm9=` differ only in pad bits and decode to the same `fo`. Python's default decoder also silently discards characters outside the alphabet, so a space and a newline vanish. `validate=True` rejects those, and the round-trip check (decode, re-encode, compare) rejects any non-canonical string, because a conforming encoder only ever produces one spelling.

Do not "fix" malformed input by cleaning it up and carrying on. Repairing an overlong sequence or dropping junk characters creates exactly the second spelling an attacker needs. Strict decoders that raise an error give every component the same answer: invalid.

**Defender view.** Prevent: use strict decoders (`bytes.decode("utf-8")` with the default `errors="strict"` at trust boundaries, `b64decode(..., validate=True)` plus a round-trip check where the encoded form matters). Detect: count decode failures per client; a burst of invalid UTF-8 or invalid base64 in URLs and tokens is someone probing your decoders. Respond: return a 400 error, log the raw bytes in hex, and check whether any other component in the path accepted what yours rejected.
An encoding is safe to check only if every value has exactly one valid spelling and every decoder rejects the rest.

blocks.question: A lenient UTF-8 decoder receives the bytes `C0 AE`. What does it return, and what should a conforming decoder do?
options: Nothing; both decoders skip unknown bytes
Two Latin-1 characters, U+00C0 and U+00AE; accept them
A replacement character; accept it silently
An overlong dot `.`; reject the sequence as invalid
blocks.explain: 110 00000 10 101110 carries the value 0x2E, a dot. RFC 3629 forbids overlongs (C0 and C1 can never appear in valid UTF-8), so a conforming decoder must raise an error rather than produce the dot.

blocks.question: Your API rejects a list of known-bad base64 tokens by comparing the token text, then decodes and uses the bytes. What is the most robust fix?
options: Also block the token with `==` appended
Decode strictly (reject junk and non-zero pad bits), then compare the decoded bytes
Lower-case tokens before comparing
Switch to hex encoding
blocks.explain: Many strings can decode to the same bytes (non-zero pad bits, ignored junk characters). Comparing the decoded bytes, after a strict decode, makes the decision on the value you will use. Adding variants one at a time never ends.

blocks.md:
Percent-encoding (from Python for security work) writes a byte as `%` and two hex digits, so `%2e` is a dot and `%25` is the percent sign itself. That last fact is the trap: `%252e` decodes once to `%2e`, and a second time to `.`.

The rule that keeps layered systems safe is simple to say: **each layer decodes exactly once, and the check runs on the value in the form the next consumer will use.** A **double decoding** bug is any design where one more decode happens after the check, so a value that looked harmless at check time becomes dangerous at use time.

**Case: IIS, 2001.** Microsoft bulletin [MS01-026](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2001/ms01-026) (14 May 2001) describes it precisely. When IIS received a request to run a program, it "performs a decoding pass to render the request in a canonical form, then performs security checks on the decoded request. A vulnerability results because a second, superfluous decoding pass is performed after the security checks are completed." A request could pass the check and then be "mapped via the second decoding pass" to a program outside the site's folders, such as an operating system command. NVD's entry for this bug, CVE-2001-0333, summarises it as encoding `..` and `\` characters twice.

blocks.code:
from urllib.parse import unquote

def handle(raw):
    once = unquote(raw)                 # decode pass 1
    if ".." in once:                    # security check
        return "403 " + once
    twice = unquote(once)               # superfluous pass 2
    return "200 open " + twice

print(handle("docs/a.txt"))
print(handle("%2e%2e/secret"))
print(handle("%252e%252e/secret"))
blocks.caption: Output: `200 open docs/a.txt` / `403 ../secret` / `200 open ../secret`

blocks.title: The superfluous second decode
blocks.code:
from urllib.parse import unquote

def handle(raw):
    once = unquote(raw)                 # decode pass 1
    if ".." in once:                    # security check
        return "403 " + once
    twice = unquote(once)               # superfluous pass 2
    return "200 open " + twice

print(handle("docs/a.txt"))
print(handle("%2e%2e/secret"))
print(handle("%252e%252e/secret"))

scenes.caption: A normal request. One decode gives `docs/a.txt`, no `..`, and the file opens.
Single-encoded dots decode to `../secret` in pass 1, and the check catches them.
Double-encoded: pass 1 turns `%25` into `%`, leaving `%2e%2e/secret`. There is still no `..` in the text, so the check passes.
The superfluous pass 2 now produces real dots after the check has already said yes.
The path that is opened is not the path that was checked. This is check-then-transform, exactly as in MS01-026.

blocks.code:
from urllib.parse import unquote

def handle(raw):
    path = unquote(raw)                 # decode exactly once
    if "%" in path:                     # leftover escapes: refuse, never decode again
        return "400 " + path
    if ".." in path.split("/"):
        return "403 " + path
    return "200 open " + path

print(handle("docs/a.txt"))
print(handle("%2e%2e/secret"))
print(handle("%252e%252e/secret"))
blocks.caption: Output: `200 open docs/a.txt` / `403 ../secret` / `400 %2e%2e/secret`. A filename containing a literal percent sign would need a different design; the point is that no layer decodes again.

blocks.md: This is the opposite of the detection advice in Python for security work, and both are right. When you *search logs*, decode repeatedly until the text stops changing, so you find every disguise. When you *enforce* a rule, decode exactly once and refuse whatever still looks encoded, so no later layer can produce a new meaning after you said yes.

**Path normalisation** is the same problem one step later. Before opening a file, servers clean the path: they resolve `.` and `..`, merge repeated slashes and, on Windows, treat `\` as a separator. If the cleaning and the access check disagree on any of these, traversal returns.

**Case: Apache HTTP Server, 2021.** [CVE-2021-41773](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-41773) was "a flaw ... in a change made to path normalization" in Apache 2.4.49 that let URLs map to files outside directories set by `Alias`-like directives, wherever the default `Require all denied` protection had been removed; with CGI enabled it could run code. It was exploited in the wild, and the [Apache advisory page](https://httpd.apache.org/security/vulnerabilities_24.html) records that the 2.4.50 fix was itself incomplete (CVE-2021-42013). CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 3 November 2021.

blocks.prompt: In the Apache case, what single configuration line limited the damage on servers that kept it, even while unpatched?
blocks.reveal: The default `Require all denied` on directories outside the ones the site serves. NVD's description says requests succeed only "if files outside of these directories are not protected by the usual default configuration". Path normalisation decided *which file*; the authorisation rule still decided *whether* it could be served. A deny-by-default filesystem policy is the layer that does not depend on any parser agreeing.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Prevent: decode once per layer; resolve paths with the platform's own function (`os.path.realpath`) and compare with `os.path.commonpath`; keep deny-by-default access rules on everything outside the served folders; patch web servers quickly, because path handling bugs are mass-scanned. Detect: alert on `%25` followed by hex in request paths, on encoded slashes or dots, and on 400 or 403 bursts from one source; for Apache, look in access logs for requests whose path reaches outside your `Alias` targets. Respond: confirm which files were served (response sizes in access logs), rotate any secrets those files held, and patch.

blocks.question: After the first decode your app sees `%2e%2e/secret`. Which response is safest for an enforcement point?
options: Reject the request because encoded characters remain after the one allowed decode
Decode again until nothing changes, then check
Strip every `%` and continue
Allow it, since it contains no `..`
blocks.explain: Decoding again inside the enforcement point is the MS01-026 mistake moved one line up. Stripping creates yet another spelling. Refusing values that still look encoded means no later layer can turn them into something you never checked.

blocks.question: Why is checking `".." in path` on the raw request weaker than resolving the path and checking where it lands?
options: Because `in` is slow on long strings
Because `..` is legal in file names
Because Python strings are immutable
Because the filesystem, not the string check, decides what `..`, separators and links finally mean
blocks.explain: Encodings, backslashes on Windows, repeated slashes and symbolic links all change where a path lands. Resolving first and checking the resolved location makes the decision on the same meaning the filesystem will use.

lessons.title: HTML character references and the order a browser decodes

blocks.md:
Inside one HTML attribute, several languages are nested. Take `<a href="...">`: the attribute value is HTML text, which holds a URL, whose scheme decides what clicking does. The browser peels these layers from the outside in, and each layer has its own decoding rules.

The outermost layer is HTML. An HTML **character reference** writes a character by name or number: `&` is `&`, `j` is `j` (decimal 106), `j` is also `j` (hex). The [HTML parsing rules](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/parsing.html) switch into a "character reference state" whenever they meet `&` inside a quoted attribute value, so references are replaced before anything else ever reads the value.

The next layer is the URL. The WHATWG (Web Hypertext Application Technology Working Group, the browser makers' standards body) [URL Standard](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) says a browser must "remove any leading and trailing C0 control or space" from the input and "remove all ASCII tab or newline" from anywhere in it. (C0 controls are the invisible characters U+0000 to U+001F.) Scheme names are also matched without regard to case.

You met the Samy worm in The browser security model. Samy Kamkar's own technical write-up records one detail that belongs here: MySpace stripped the word `javascript` from profiles, but some browsers of 2005 read `java` + newline + `script` as `javascript` inside a CSS `url(...)` value. A filter and a browser disagreed about what a newline inside a scheme means. Today's URL Standard makes dropping that newline the official rule for every browser.

blocks.code:
import html, re

def naive_filter(href):                     # looks at the raw attribute text
    return "javascript:" not in href.lower()

def browser_view(href):                     # simplified model of the browser
    s = html.unescape(href)                 # 1. HTML parser decodes &...; refs
    s = re.sub(r"[\t\n\r]", "", s)          # 2. URL parser drops tab/newline
    s = s.strip("".join(map(chr, range(0x21))))  # and leading/trailing C0 + space
    return s.split(":", 1)[0].lower()       # 3. the scheme it will act on

for href in ["https://a.example/", "javascript:go()",
             "java	script:go()", "javascript:go()"]:
    print(f"{href:24} filter_ok={naive_filter(href)!s:5} scheme={browser_view(href)}")
blocks.caption: Output: the first two rows match the filter's view; for the last two the filter says True but the browser model still finds the scheme `javascript`. `go()` stands in for any script.

blocks.title: One attribute, three decoders, peeled from the outside in

scenes.caption: What the filter sees: the raw attribute text. No `javascript:` substring appears, so it passes.
Layer 1, the HTML parser: the character reference `	` becomes a real tab character (U+0009).
Layer 2, the URL parser: the Standard removes every ASCII tab or newline, so the tab disappears.
Layer 3: the scheme is now `javascript`, and clicking would run script. The check ran on layer 0; the action used layer 3.

blocks.md:
The lesson is not "also block tabs". A blocklist would have to model every decoder in the browser, in the right order, forever. The fix flips the direction of the work:

1. Treat the user's URL as **plain text**, never as ready-made HTML.
2. Parse it with a real URL parser and **allow** only the schemes you want (`http`, `https`), with a host.
3. Encode it for the HTML attribute context on output, so the browser's HTML decoding gives back exactly the text you checked.

blocks.caption: Output: `link` / `REJECTED scheme not allowed: 'javascript'` / `REJECTED scheme not allowed: ''`

blocks.md:
Why it works: step 3 means the browser's layer-1 decode can only undo your own encoding (`&` back to `&`), never introduce a new character, so layer 2 sees precisely the string that passed step 2. The third input shows the other half: written as text, `javascript:` has no valid scheme at all, and after encoding the browser would show it literally as `j...` rather than decoding it.

Template engines that auto-escape attributes do step 3 for you; the scheme allowlist (step 2) they usually do not. Encoding rules per context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL) are covered in the course XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks, lesson "Context decides the encoding: body, attribute, JavaScript, URL". As a second layer, the CSP lesson in The browser security model showed that a policy with `script-src` set blocks `javascript:` URLs unless you explicitly allow them.
Decoding order is outside-in: HTML first, then URL, then script. Check the innermost value as plain data, then encode it for each outer layer on the way out.

**Defender view.** Prevent: scheme allowlists on every user-supplied link, auto-escaping templates, and a CSP without `'unsafe-inline'`. Detect: CSP violation reports (the `report-to` or `report-uri` endpoint) naming `inline` sources on pages that show user links; stored values containing `&#` or control characters in fields meant to be URLs. Respond: find every stored record with a non-http(s) scheme after real URL parsing, neutralise them, and review which pages rendered them.

blocks.question: A filter rejects attributes whose text contains `javascript:`. Which attribute text gets past it but still produces a `javascript` scheme in the browser?
options: `https://a.example/javascript:`
`JAVASCRIPT:go()` after the filter lower-cases
`javascript:go()`
`javascript%3Ago()`
blocks.explain: The HTML parser turns `j` into `j` before the URL parser runs. The https URL only has `javascript:` in its path (and the filter blocks it anyway). A lower-casing filter catches `JAVASCRIPT:`. In `javascript%3Ago()`, `%3A` is not decoded when the scheme is parsed, so there is no `javascript:` scheme.

blocks.question: Why should the scheme check run on the plain-text URL and not on the HTML you are about to output?
options: Plain text is shorter, so the check is faster
The plain-text value is what the browser's URL parser will see once it undoes your HTML encoding
Browsers ignore schemes in encoded HTML
HTML encoding removes the scheme
blocks.explain: Your attribute encoding is undone exactly once by the browser's HTML parser. Checking the plain value and then encoding it means the URL parser sees the same string your check approved.

lessons.title: Unicode normalisation: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD

blocks.md:
`é` can be stored two ways: as one code point, U+00E9 (LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE), or as two, `e` (U+0065) followed by U+0301 (COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT). They look identical and mean the same thing, yet `==` in Python says they differ, because it compares code points.

**Normalisation** fixes that by converting text to one agreed form. It is defined in Unicode Standard Annex #15 (UAX: a Unicode Standard Annex, part of the standard itself), [Unicode Normalization Forms](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr15/). UAX #15 defines two kinds of sameness:

- **Canonical equivalence**: the same abstract character, which "when correctly displayed should always have the same visual appearance and behavior". The two `é` spellings are canonically equivalent, as are the OHM SIGN Ω (U+2126) and the Greek capital omega Ω (U+03A9).
- **Compatibility equivalence**: a weaker kind, where forms "may have distinct visual appearances or behaviors": the `ﬁ` ligature and `fi`, a superscript `⁵` and `5`, fullwidth `／` and `/`.

That gives four forms:

- **NFD**: canonical decomposition (split `é` into `e` + accent).
- **NFC**: canonical decomposition, then canonical composition (put it back together as U+00E9).
- **NFKD** and **NFKC**: the same, but using compatibility decomposition too, so `ﬁ` becomes `f` + `i` and `／` becomes `/`.

NF stands for Normalization Form; D for decomposition, C for composition. UAX #15 explains the K: "a K is used to stand for compatibility to avoid confusion with the C standing for composition". Every form is **idempotent**, meaning applying it twice gives the same result as once: `toNFKC(toNFKC(x)) = toNFKC(x)`.

blocks.code:
from unicodedata import normalize, name

samples = ["é", "é", "Ω", "ﬁ", "／", "⁵", "ᴮ"]
for s in samples:
    print(" + ".join(f"U+{ord(c):04X}" for c in s).ljust(15),
          [normalize(f, s) for f in ("NFC", "NFD", "NFKC")],
          [f"U+{ord(c):04X}" for c in normalize("NFKC", s)])
print("é" == "é", normalize("NFC", "é") == normalize("NFC", "é"))
blocks.caption: Output, one line per sample (code points, then [NFC, NFD, NFKC], then the NFKC code points): `é` stays one code point; `e` + U+0301 composes to U+00E9; the ohm sign becomes U+03A9 even under NFC; `ﬁ`, `／`, `⁵` and `ᴮ` change only under NFKC (to `fi`, `/`, `5`, `B`). Last line: `False True`.

blocks.title: Six inputs through NFC and NFKC

scenes.caption: Six inputs, written as code points. The first two look identical on screen; so do the third and a Greek omega.
NFC merges canonical equivalents: both `é` spellings become U+00E9 and the ohm sign becomes omega. Compatibility characters are left alone.
NFKC also folds compatibility forms: the ligature splits into f and i, fullwidth solidus becomes `/` (U+002F), modifier ᴮ becomes B.
The red cells are the dangerous ones: NFKC can create ASCII syntax characters such as `/` from characters a check never thought were special.

blocks.md: Normalisation is good: [RFC 3629](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3629.txt) points out that many spellings of "the same thing" affect matching, and that normalisation is the remedy. The bug is normalising **after** the check. NFKC turns characters with no special meaning into `/`, `.`, `:` and `@`, so a check on the raw text and an action on the normalised text see different strings.

blocks.caption: Output: `'../config'` / `good: bad name`. The input is fullwidth full stop, fullwidth full stop, fullwidth solidus, then `config`.

blocks.md: **Case: Python's own URL parser, 2019.** [CVE-2019-9636](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2019-9636) affected `urllib.parse.urlsplit` and `urlparse`: "Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding (with an incorrect netloc) during NFKC normalization", and NVD says a crafted URL "could be incorrectly parsed to locate cookies or authentication data and send that information to a different host than when parsed correctly". The cause was characters in the host part that NFKC, which IDNA host encoding applies, turns into URL delimiters. The fix, documented in the [urllib.parse docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.parse.html), makes `urlsplit` raise `ValueError` when characters in the host part decompose under NFKC into `/`, `?`, `#`, `@` or `:`. Python itself normalises source code this way: the language reference says "all names are converted into the normalization form NFKC while parsing", so `ｘ` and `x` are the same variable.

UAX #15: "Normalization Forms KC and KD must not be blindly applied to arbitrary text", because they erase distinctions that can matter. Use NFKC (usually with case folding, next lesson) for identifiers such as usernames, and NFC for stored text you will show back to people.

**Defender view.** Prevent: normalise first, then validate, then use the normalised value everywhere; or reject any identifier that is not already in normal form (`s != normalize("NFKC", s)`), which keeps one spelling per value. Detect: log when an input changes under normalisation in security-relevant fields (paths, hostnames, usernames); legitimate users rarely type fullwidth punctuation. Respond: re-run your validation over stored data in normalised form to find records that were accepted under the old order.

blocks.question: Which pair is canonically equivalent (so equal after NFC), not just compatibility equivalent?
options: `ﬁ` (U+FB01) and `fi`
`／` (U+FF0F) and `/`
Ω OHM SIGN (U+2126) and Ω GREEK CAPITAL LETTER OMEGA (U+03A9)
blocks.explain: UAX #15 lists the ohm sign as a canonical singleton: it never survives normalisation, even NFC. The ligature, fullwidth solidus and superscript five are compatibility equivalents and change only under NFKC or NFKD.

blocks.question: A file name check rejects `/` and `..`, then the code stores `normalize("NFKC", name)`. What is wrong?
options: NFKC can produce `/` and `.` from fullwidth characters after the check has run
Nothing; NFKC only changes accents
NFKC is slower than NFC
NFKC turns file names upper-case
blocks.explain: Fullwidth full stop and fullwidth solidus normalise to `.` and `/`. Normalise first, then check the normalised value, then use that same value.

lessons.title: Case mapping and case folding: when lower() is not one-to-one

blocks.md:
For ASCII, upper and lower case are a neat pairing: 26 letters each way, one to one. Unicode case mapping is not. Some characters become two characters, some characters from different alphabets end up as the same letter, and some have no case at all.

- **Case mapping** (`upper()`, `lower()`) converts text for display.
- **Case folding** (`casefold()` in Python) is a separate mapping designed for caseless *comparison*: it is more aggressive, folding `ß` to `ss`, for instance.

blocks.code:
cases = ["ß", "İ", "ı", "K", "ﬁ", "ς"]
for s in cases:
    print(f"U+{ord(s):04X} {s!r:6} upper={s.upper()!r:6} lower={s.lower()!r:9} "
          f"casefold={s.casefold()!r:6} len(lower)={len(s.lower())}")
blocks.caption: Output: ß upper-cases to `SS` (one character becomes two); İ (capital I with dot) lower-cases to two code points, `i` + U+0307; dotless ı upper-cases to plain ASCII `I`; the KELVIN SIGN lower-cases to ASCII `k`; `ﬁ` upper-cases to `FI`; final sigma ς case-folds to σ.

blocks.md:
Read the dotless ı row twice. It is a different letter from `i` (it belongs to Turkish and Azerbaijani), yet `"ı".upper()` is `"I"`, the same as `"i".upper()`. So two strings that differ can become equal after `upper()`. Likewise the KELVIN SIGN (U+212A) and ASCII `K` both lower-case to `k`.

That breaks a common pattern: "find the account whose email matches, ignoring case". Databases do this with `UPPER(email) = UPPER(?)` or with case-insensitive collations (collation: the database's rules for comparing and sorting text), and those rules may treat distinct strings as equal.

**Case: Django, December 2019.** Django is a popular Python web framework. Its [security release](https://www.djangoproject.com/weblog/2019/dec/18/security-releases/) for CVE-2019-19844 explains that the password-reset form used a case-insensitive query, so an attacker who knew a victim's address could "craft an email address which is distinct from the address associated with that account" but which "ceases to be distinct after case transformation" of Unicode characters. The reset email went to the address the attacker typed, so the attacker received a valid token for someone else's account. The team says the reporter, Simon Charette, noticed it after reading about a similar issue affecting GitHub.

Django's fix had two parts: after the database match, re-check equality in Python using the identifier comparison recommended by Unicode Technical Report #36 (apply NFKC, then case folding), and send the email to the address stored in the database, never the one submitted.

blocks.caption: Output: `token for admin@corp.example mailed to admın@corp.example` / `no account` / `token for admin@corp.example mailed to admin@corp.example`. The attempt uses dotless ı (U+0131).

blocks.title: A reset request with a dotless i

scenes.caption: The attacker asks for a reset for `admın@corp.example`, with a dotless ı. It is a different address that the attacker can receive mail at.
The case-insensitive lookup upper-cases both sides. ı and i both become I, so the admin's row matches.

note.text: ı and i both give I

scenes.caption: Vulnerable: the token for the admin account is mailed to the address the attacker typed.
Fixed version (the red arrow above was the old behaviour): re-compare NFKC + casefold in code (ı stays ı, so no match) and only ever mail the stored address.

blocks.md:
Why both halves of the fix matter. The Python re-check removes the false match, so a lookalike address no longer finds the account. Sending to the stored address is the deeper fix: even if some future comparison bug matches the wrong row, the token goes to the real owner. Design rule: **a message that proves control of an address must go to the address on record**, not to user input.

Also enforce one canonical form at sign-up. Store a unique index on `casefold(NFKC(email))` (or the same for usernames) so two accounts can never differ only by case or compatibility form.

Locale-aware case mapping makes it worse: in Turkish, `I` lower-cases to dotless ı. Code that lower-cases with the server's locale can give different answers on different machines. For identifiers, use locale-independent case folding, as Python's `str.casefold()` is.

**Defender view.** Prevent: compare identifiers as `casefold(NFKC(x))` and enforce uniqueness on that form; send verification and reset messages only to stored addresses. Detect: password-reset requests whose submitted address is not byte-for-byte equal to the stored one; sign-ups whose canonical form collides with an existing account. Respond: invalidate outstanding reset tokens, review resets where the delivery address differed from the stored address, and notify affected users.

blocks.question: Which pair of different strings compares equal after `.upper()`?
options: `1` and `l`
`a` and `á`
`ı` (dotless i) and `i`
`ß` and `s`
blocks.explain: Both `ı` and `i` upper-case to `I`. Accents survive case mapping (`á` gives `Á`), digits have no case, and `ß` upper-cases to `SS`, which is two letters, not one `S`.

blocks.question: In Django's CVE-2019-19844 fix, why send the reset email to the stored address rather than the submitted one?
options: Stored addresses are already lower-case, so mail delivery is faster
The submitted address might contain spaces
It guarantees the token reaches the account's real owner even if the matching step is fooled
SMTP servers reject Unicode addresses
blocks.explain: The matching logic decides which account the token is for; the delivery address decides who receives it. Tying delivery to the stored address means a matching bug can at worst send the owner an unexpected email.

lessons.title: Canonical identifiers and idempotence: the Spotify takeover

blocks.md: Services that let people pick a username usually keep two versions of it. The **verbatim** name is what the person typed, kept for display. The **canonical** name is a standard form used for uniqueness and lookup, so `BigBird` and `bigbird` cannot be two different accounts. The function that makes the canonical name must have one property above all: it must be **idempotent**, meaning that applying it twice gives the same result as applying it once. Services pass usernames between many internal systems, and each may canonicalise "just to be safe". If a second application changes the name, two systems will be talking about two different accounts.

**Case: Spotify.** In a June 2013 post on the [Spotify engineering blog](https://engineering.atspotify.com/2013/06/creative-usernames/), Spotify's Mikael Goldmann describes an incident from "some years" earlier. Late on Good Friday, a user posted on the support forum that they could hijack accounts; within minutes the forum manager's account had a new password. The steps, as the post lists them: register a new account whose name is the victim's name written in modifier capital letters, `ᴮᴵᴳᴮᴵᴿᴰ` for a victim called `bigbird`; request a password reset for the new account; use the link from your own mailbox; then log in as `bigbird` with the new password.

Spotify canonicalised with `nodeprep`, a profile from XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol, a chat standard) implemented in the Twisted Python framework. Applied once, it turned `ᴮᴵᴳᴮᴵᴿᴰ` into `BIGBIRD`. Applied again, it gave `bigbird`.

scenes.caption: Registration canonicalises once: ᴮᴵᴳᴮᴵᴿᴰ becomes BIGBIRD, which does not collide with the existing bigbird, so a new account is created.
The reset request canonicalises once again, finds the BIGBIRD account, and mails its link to the attacker's own address.
Using the link canonicalises the stored name BIGBIRD one more time. The non-idempotent function now yields bigbird.
The new password lands on the victim's account. Every step used the same function; it simply was not idempotent.

blocks.md:
Why was nodeprep not idempotent? The post traced it down two layers. The nodeprep draft defines its tables for Unicode 3.2 input only, and the modifier letters are not in Unicode 3.2; neither the draft, Twisted, nor Spotify checked that. Worse, the bug "was not actually there from the start": Twisted relied on Python's `unicodedata` module, which raised an error for such input in Python 2.4 but not in 2.5. An interpreter upgrade silently removed a safety check. Twisted fixed the issue in version 11.0.0.

The IETF later replaced this whole family of string-preparation rules. [RFC 8264](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8264.txt), the PRECIS framework (Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings), notes that its predecessor Stringprep "was tied to Unicode version 3.2", and warns that applying its own rules is "not necessarily an idempotent procedure", because NFKC after case mapping "can still yield uppercase characters".

blocks.code:
from unicodedata import normalize

def canon(name):                    # toy: lower-case, THEN NFKC
    return normalize("NFKC", name.lower())

typed = "ᴮᴵᴳᴮᴵᴿᴰ"   # modifier capitals
once = canon(typed)
twice = canon(once)
print(typed, "->", once, "->", twice)
print("idempotent?", once == twice)

def canon_fixed(name):              # NFKC, case fold, repeat until stable
    for _ in range(4):              # first pass + up to 3 more (RFC 8264)
        nxt = normalize("NFKC", normalize("NFKC", name).casefold())
        if nxt == name:
            return name
        name = nxt
    raise ValueError("unstable name")

def can_register(name):             # Spotify's stopgap: only fixpoints
    return canon(canon(name)) == canon(name)

print(canon_fixed(typed), can_register(typed), can_register("bigbird"))
blocks.caption: Output: `ᴮᴵᴳᴮᴵᴿᴰ -> BIGBIRD -> bigbird` / `idempotent? False` / `bigbird False True`. The toy `canon` lower-cases before NFKC, which reproduces the non-idempotence.

blocks.md:
Look at the output. `"ᴮ".lower()` changes nothing, because modifier letters have no lower-case form; NFKC then turns them into ASCII capitals. A second pass lower-cases those. Two defences appear in the code:

- `canon_fixed` follows RFC 8264: "apply the rules repeatedly until the output string is stable", and if it has not settled after three more applications, reject the input.
- `can_register` is Spotify's own fix: reject any name for which applying the function twice differs from applying it once. Spotify's first stopgap, used to reopen registration within hours, was stricter still: allow a username only if it is already equal to its own canonical form.

Spotify's post adds that the affected accounts were easy to find afterwards: look for accounts whose stored canonical name was not a fixed point, and each one pointed at a hijacked account.

Test canonicalisation functions for idempotence (`f(f(x)) == f(x)`) on every input you accept, and refuse inputs that fail. Store and compare only the canonical form; never re-canonicalise an already-canonical value and expect it to stay put unless that property is enforced.

[RFC 8265](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8265.txt), the PRECIS profile for usernames, shows a full modern recipe for its case-insensitive profile: map fullwidth and halfwidth characters to their normal width, allow only PRECIS identifier characters, then apply case mapping, normalisation and a directionality rule in that order, and finally make sure the result is not empty (a non-empty input can canonicalise to nothing). The order is specified because, as this lesson shows, the order changes the answer.

**Defender view.** Prevent: one shared canonicalisation library for every service, an idempotence check at sign-up, a unique index on the canonical column, and a regression test that pins behaviour across language and library upgrades (Spotify's bug arrived with an upgrade). Detect: periodically scan for stored canonical names where `f(stored) != stored`; alert on password resets where the canonical name of the reset target differs from that of the account changed. Respond: as Spotify did, close registration if needed, find non-fixed-point accounts, restore the victims, and reward the reporters (the post says the two users got premium months).

blocks.question: Which property, missing from Spotify's canonicalisation, made the takeover possible?
options: Collision resistance, like a hash function
Idempotence: applying it twice must give the same result as once
Reversibility: the verbatim name must be recoverable
Speed: it must run in constant time
blocks.explain: The name was canonicalised at registration, at the reset request and again when the link was used. Because a second pass changed BIGBIRD into bigbird, the third step addressed a different account.

blocks.prompt: Spotify's interim fix allowed a new username only if it equalled its own canonical form. Would `BigBird` (ASCII, mixed case) pass that rule?
blocks.reveal: No. Its canonical form is `bigbird`, which differs from what was typed, so the stopgap refused it even though it is harmless. That is the trade-off of a fixed-point rule: very safe, slightly unfriendly. The later fix, rejecting only names where `f(f(x)) != f(x)`, accepts `BigBird`, because `f(f("BigBird"))` and `f("BigBird")` are both `bigbird`.

blocks.question: RFC 8264 says to reapply PRECIS rules until the output is stable. What should happen if it is still changing after three extra rounds?
options: Reject the input string as invalid
Fall back to ASCII lower-casing
Use the last output anyway
Keep applying the rules until it stops
blocks.explain: The RFC says the implementation "SHOULD terminate application of the rules and reject the input string as invalid". Looping forever would be a denial-of-service risk, and accepting an unstable value recreates the Spotify bug.

lessons.title: Lossy conversion: Windows Best-Fit and PHP CVE-2024-4577

blocks.md:
Not every system speaks Unicode end to end. Windows keeps two versions of many functions: Unicode ones with a `W` suffix for "wide" characters (UTF-16), such as `GetEnvironmentVariableW`, and ones with an `A` suffix for "ANSI" (American National Standards Institute: Microsoft says code page 1252 was based on an ANSI draft, and the name stuck), such as `GetEnvironmentVariableA`, that use the system's **ANSI code page** (ACP), a legacy character set of 8 to 16 bits per character chosen by the system's language settings (for example code page 932 for Japanese). When text crosses from the wide world into the ANSI world, characters the code page cannot represent must become something.

Windows can apply **Best-Fit** mapping: instead of `?`, it substitutes a character that looks or means about the same. That is friendly for displaying text. It is a disaster when the converted text is then *parsed*, because Best-Fit can create syntax characters that were not there when the input was checked.

Orange Tsai and splitline of DEVCORE, a Taiwanese security firm, documented this in their January 2025 research WorstFit. Examples from it, each visible in Microsoft's own [best-fit tables](https://www.unicode.org/Public/MAPPINGS/VENDORS/MICSFT/WindowsBestFit/):

- U+00AD SOFT HYPHEN (an invisible hint where a word may be hyphenated) becomes `-` on the Chinese (936, 950) and Japanese (932) code pages.
- U+00A5 YEN SIGN becomes `\` on the Japanese code page 932, but `Y` on the Central European code page 1250, and stays unchanged on most others.
- Fullwidth forms such as U+FF0F `／` become `/`, and U+FF02 `＂` becomes `"` on code pages 125x and 874.

They also note the behaviour had been raised before, in Chris Weber's talk "Unicode Security" at Black Hat USA 2009 (Black Hat: a large annual security research conference).

blocks.title: A check on the wide string, an action on the narrow one

scenes.caption: The web server receives a query string containing U+00AD, a soft hyphen, followed by text.
Simplified model: the program checks for a leading `-` before the conversion. U+00AD is not `-`, so the check passes.
The command line is converted to the ANSI code page. On 932, 936 or 950, Best-Fit maps the soft hyphen to `-`.
The child process parses its ANSI arguments and finds an option the check meant to forbid.
Fixes: stay wide end to end (W APIs, UTF-8 process code page), or convert first and check the converted bytes, refusing input the conversion changed.

blocks.md: **Case: PHP-CGI, June 2024.** PHP can run as a CGI program (Common Gateway Interface: the web server starts a program per request and passes it the request). Since a 2012 bug, CVE-2012-1823, PHP-CGI has carried a protection meant to stop query strings being read as command-line options. DEVCORE reported on 7 May 2024 that on Windows this protection could be bypassed: per [NVD's CVE-2024-4577](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-4577), when PHP-CGI runs under Apache on Windows with certain code pages, "Windows may use 'Best-Fit' behavior to replace characters in command line", and PHP "may misinterpret those characters as PHP options", which can reveal source code or run arbitrary PHP code. DEVCORE's [alert](https://devco.re/blog/2024/06/06/security-alert-cve-2024-4577-php-cgi-argument-injection-vulnerability-en/) names Chinese and Japanese code pages and notes that XAMPP for Windows (an Apache and PHP bundle) was vulnerable in its default configuration. Fixed versions shipped on 6 June 2024; CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 12 June 2024.

blocks.caption: Output: `['tool.exe', '-v']` / `refused: conversion changed the argument`. A toy: the three-entry table is illustrative, not a real code page, and `tool.exe` stands for any program.

blocks.md: Why `launch_good` works: it checks the string the child process will actually read, after the lossy step, and refuses any input that conversion altered. Even better is to remove the lossy step: call wide APIs end to end, set the process to the UTF-8 code page, and never build a command line from request data at all. WorstFit's own conclusion is that this is an operating-system-level problem that will keep reappearing until ANSI conversions are phased out, so the durable fix is to stop depending on them.

Escaping does not save you here. WorstFit shows arguments that were correctly quoted and escaped in UTF-16 becoming mis-split after conversion, because a fullwidth quote or a yen sign turns into a real quote or backslash after the escaping already ran.

**Defender view.** Prevent: patch PHP; do not expose `php-cgi` directly (use PHP-FPM, PHP's FastCGI Process Manager, or a module); in your own Windows code, use W APIs and the UTF-8 code page; never pass request data as process arguments. Detect: web logs with a soft hyphen (the byte `%AD`, which DEVCORE's temporary rewrite rule matched at the start of the query string, or `%C2%AD` in UTF-8) or fullwidth punctuation in query strings sent to CGI paths; process creation events (Windows Security event [4688](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-4688), with command-line logging enabled) showing `php-cgi.exe` started with option-style arguments your configuration never passes. Respond: treat a hit as possible code execution: isolate the host, review what PHP ran, rotate secrets the server held.

blocks.question: In the toy, why does the check `arg.startswith("-")` miss the attack?
options: Python's `startswith` ignores invisible characters
The child process strips the first character
The soft hyphen is a dash in every encoding
The check runs on the wide string, and only the later ANSI conversion turns U+00AD into `-`
blocks.explain: At check time the first character is U+00AD, which is not `-`. Best-Fit mapping happens afterwards, on the way to the ANSI command line, so the check and the child see different strings.

blocks.question: Which change removes this whole class of bug from a Windows program, rather than patching one character?
options: Add U+00AD to a blocklist
Use the wide (W) APIs and UTF-8 end to end so no lossy ANSI conversion happens
Upper-case all arguments before checking
Escape arguments twice
blocks.explain: Blocklists miss the next mapped character (yen sign, fullwidth quote, and more across many code pages). Removing the lossy conversion removes the second meaning.

blocks.md:
Some characters are drawn so alike that people cannot tell them apart: Latin `a` (U+0061) and Cyrillic `а` (U+0430), Latin `o` and Greek `ο`, or the pair `rn` and `m` in many fonts. Characters like these are called **homoglyphs** (glyph: the drawn shape of a character), and strings built from them are **confusables**. Unlike every earlier lesson, no decoder disagrees here: the computer sees two different strings perfectly well. The differential is between the computer and the human reading the screen.

Unicode's answer is [UTS #39, Unicode Security Mechanisms](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr39/) (UTS: Unicode Technical Standard, a separate specification that builds on the core standard). It ships a data file, `confusables.txt`, mapping each character to a **prototype**: one or more exemplar characters it can be mistaken for. For example, the line `0441 ; 0063 ; MA` maps U+0441 CYRILLIC SMALL LETTER ES to U+0063 LATIN SMALL LETTER C (the third field is obsolete and always reads MA).

From that data UTS #39 defines a **skeleton**. The internal skeleton of a string X is computed as follows:

1. Convert X to NFD.
2. Remove characters with the property Default_Ignorable_Code_Point (invisible ones such as zero-width spaces).
3. Replace each character by its prototype.
4. Apply NFD again.

The full skeleton first reorders the string for display with the bidi algorithm (lesson 11). Two strings are **confusable** exactly when their skeletons are equal. The standard then names three classes: **single-script** confusables (the same script, like Croatian `ǉeto` and `ljeto`), **mixed-script** (no script in common, like `paypal` with two Cyrillic `а`), and **whole-script** (each string is itself in a single script, like Latin `scope` and Cyrillic `ѕсоре`).

blocks.caption: Output, one line per pair (a, b, skeleton(a), skeleton(b), confusable?): `paypal pаypаl paypal paypal True` / `scope ѕсоре scope scope True` / `rn m rn rn True` / `admin adm1n adrnin adrnln False` / `bob bab bob bab False`. Download confusables.txt from unicode.org/Public/security/latest/ first.

blocks.title: Computing a skeleton, one character at a time

scenes.caption: Input: `pаypаl`, where positions 1 and 4 are Cyrillic а (U+0430). On screen it is indistinguishable from paypal.
The script of each character. Mixed Latin and Cyrillic in one word is already suspicious, which is the idea behind restriction levels.
confusables.txt maps U+0430 to U+0061 (Latin a). Every other letter is its own prototype.
skeleton(pаypаl) equals skeleton(paypal), so UTS #39 calls them confusable: a mixed-script confusable, since their script sets share nothing.

blocks.md:
Skeletons are a comparison key, not a display form: `skeleton("m")` is `rn`, which nobody would show to a user. UTS #55 (Unicode Source Code Handling) advises treating the skeleton operation "as a black box", because it is not defined code point by code point.

The other tool is **restriction levels**: UTS #39 grades a string as ASCII-Only, Single Script, Highly Restrictive (Latin plus Han with Japanese kana, Bopomofo or Korean Hangul), Moderately Restrictive (Latin plus one other recommended script, except Cyrillic or Greek), Minimally Restrictive, or Unrestricted. A username policy of "Moderately Restrictive or better" stops `pаypаl` (Latin plus Cyrillic) but not the all-Cyrillic `ѕсоре`, which is why whole-script confusables need the skeleton check too.

**Confusables in source code.** Nicholas Boucher and Ross Anderson of the University of Cambridge, the Trojan Source researchers of lesson 11, also showed functions whose names differ only by a homoglyph, for example `sayHello` and the same name with a Cyrillic `Н`; a malicious dependency can define the lookalike and the victim calls it. That is [CVE-2021-42694](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2021-42694). Rust, which allowed non-ASCII identifiers from version 1.53.0, shipped mitigations at the same time: its compiler warns by default about `confusable_idents` and `mixed_script_confusables`. UTS #55 recommends linters warn when an identifier is confusable with another relevant identifier, and describes the Rust compiler as implementing such a check across a whole crate (Rust's unit of compilation, such as one library).

Lookalike domains in phishing use the same data; the course Phishing, social engineering and email security covers them in "Lookalike domains and homoglyphs". The next lesson covers how browsers decide whether to show a domain in Unicode at all.

**Defender view.** Prevent: at sign-up, reject usernames and project names whose skeleton equals the skeleton of an existing or reserved name (`admin`, `support`, your brand); require Moderately Restrictive or better for identifiers; in code, keep the compiler's confusable warnings on and fail CI on them. Detect: report new accounts, packages or repositories whose skeleton collides with a popular one. Respond: suspend the lookalike, warn users who interacted with it, and add its skeleton to the reserved list.

blocks.question: `ѕсоре` is written entirely in Cyrillic and `scope` entirely in Latin. Which check flags the pair?
options: A mixed-script check on each string
Comparing their NFKC forms
Comparing their UTS #39 skeletons
Comparing them after `casefold()`
blocks.explain: Each string is single-script, so a mixed-script rule passes both. NFKC and case folding leave Cyrillic letters Cyrillic. Only the skeleton, which maps Cyrillic ѕ, с, о, р, е to Latin prototypes, shows they look the same.

blocks.question: Why should you not display or store the skeleton as the user's name?
options: Skeletons are a comparison key that can change the visible text, for example m becomes rn
Skeletons are encrypted
Skeletons are always upper-case
Skeletons remove all digits
blocks.explain: A skeleton maps characters to look-alike prototypes, which may be different characters or even sequences (`m` to `rn`). Keep the canonical name for identity and use the skeleton only to detect collisions.

lessons.title: Internationalised domain names, Punycode and what browsers show

blocks.md:
DNS, the system that turns names into addresses, was built for ASCII letters, digits and hyphens. **IDNs** (internationalised domain names) allow other scripts by converting each label (the parts between dots) to an ASCII form before any DNS lookup. The conversion is called **Punycode**, defined in [RFC 3492](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3492.txt) as "a Bootstring encoding of Unicode", and the converted label gets the prefix `xn--`, marking an ASCII-Compatible Encoding (ACE). The [Chromium IDN page](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/idn.md) gives the example `öbb.at` becoming `xn--bb-eka.at`.

The rules for which characters are allowed and how they are mapped before Punycode are called IDNA (Internationalized Domain Names in Applications), and there are three versions in use: IDNA2003, IDNA2008 ([RFC 5891](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5891.txt), which obsoleted the 2003 protocol in 2010), and Unicode's UTS #46, a compatibility layer that browsers use. They do not agree.

blocks.code:
for host in ["öbb.at", "аpple.com", "аррӏе.com",
             "ⓖⓞⓞⓖⓛⓔ.com", "EXAMPLE.com"]:
    print(f"{host:12} -> {host.encode('idna').decode()}")
print(b"xn--80ak6aa92e.com".decode("idna"))
blocks.caption: Output: `öbb.at       -> xn--bb-eka.at` / `аpple.com    -> xn--pple-43d.com` / `аррӏе.com    -> xn--80ak6aa92e.com` / `ⓖⓞⓞⓖⓛⓔ.com   -> google.com` / `EXAMPLE.com  -> EXAMPLE.com` / `аррӏе.com`. Python's built-in `idna` codec implements IDNA2003 (RFC 3490).

blocks.md: The fourth line is the surprise. IDNA2003 maps the circled letters `ⓖⓞⓞⓖⓛⓔ` to plain `google`, and so does the browser's URL parser (Node's WHATWG `URL` gives `google.com` too). IDNA2008 rejects them: the third-party `idna` package, which [Python's codec docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/codecs.html) recommend if you need IDNA2008, raises `Codepoint U+24D6 at position 1 of 'ⓖⓞⓞⓖⓛⓔ' not allowed`, unless you switch on its UTS #46 mode, which again returns `google.com`. Orange Tsai's Black Hat USA 2017 talk used this exact example: a URL checker and a URL fetcher using different IDNA versions see different hosts.

scenes.caption: 1 means the processor accepts the name and produces an ASCII host; 0 means it raises an error. Ordinary IDNs like öbb.at work everywhere.
The circled-letter name: IDNA2003 and UTS #46 (used by browsers) map it to google.com, while IDNA2008 rejects it. A checker and a fetcher built on different rows disagree.
The Cyrillic lookalikes are valid under all three. Encoding cannot protect people here; that job falls to the display policy below.

blocks.md: **Case: the apple.com lookalike, 2017.** Xudong Zheng, a security researcher, [registered](https://www.xudongz.com/blog/2017/idn-phishing/) `xn--80ak6aa92e.com`, which is `аррӏе.com` spelled entirely in Cyrillic. Browsers already showed *mixed-script* labels such as `xn--pple-43d.com` as Punycode, but this label was single-script, so Chrome, Firefox and Opera displayed it as Unicode, indistinguishable from apple.com. Zheng reported it to Chrome and Firefox on 20 January 2017. Chrome fixed it that spring. Mozilla declined at the time, writing that its IDN threat model "specifically excludes whole-script homographs"; Zheng suggested users set `network.IDN_show_punycode` to true. Zheng also reported that Safari was not vulnerable.

Each browser now runs its own **display policy** on every label. Chromium's documented algorithm includes, among other steps: show Punycode if a label mixes scripts beyond UTS #39's Highly Restrictive profile (with Latin, Cyrillic and Greek never mixed); if it contains invisible characters or mixed digit systems; if it is a **whole-script confusable** (for example all Cyrillic lookalike letters) under a TLD (top-level domain, the last label such as `com`) not associated with that script; or if its UTS #39 skeleton matches one of a list of top domains. Firefox's [IDN display algorithm](https://wiki.mozilla.org/IDN_Display_Algorithm) is based on UTS #39's Moderately Restrictive profile, plus a list of TLDs whose registries have anti-spoofing policies.

Chromium's page is blunt that this is not a complete defence: it calls homographs "a limitation of how URLs are displayed in browsers in general" and lists other protections, such as Safe Browsing warnings and password managers that will not fill a password into a domain that is not exactly the right one. Treat the address bar as a hint, not a guarantee.

**Defender view.** Prevent: register the obvious Punycode lookalikes of your main domains; use phishing-resistant sign-in (passkeys bind to the exact domain); in your own software, decide which IDNA version you implement and use the same one for checking and fetching. Detect: watch newly registered domains and certificate issuance for names whose skeleton (after Punycode decoding) matches yours. Respond: report lookalikes to the registrar and to browser safe-browsing services, and warn users.

blocks.question: Your URL allowlist uses an IDNA2008 library and rejects `ⓖⓞⓞⓖⓛⓔ.com`, but your HTTP client uses UTS #46. What is the risk, and what is the fix?
options: No risk: rejection is always safe
Punycode is reversible, so there is no risk
The client will send circled letters to DNS
The two components disagree about which names are valid and what they map to; use one library for both checking and fetching
blocks.explain: Here the checker is stricter, which happens to fail safe, but the pair still disagree; reverse the roles and a name the checker passes could reach a different host. Parse once with the library the fetcher uses, then check that result.

blocks.question: Why did Chrome's 2017 mixed-script rule fail against `аррӏе.com`?
options: Chrome did not support Punycode
The letters were fullwidth
The domain used a Cyrillic TLD
The label was entirely Cyrillic, so it was not mixed-script: a whole-script confusable
blocks.explain: Mixed-script rules catch Latin plus Cyrillic in one label. A label written only in Cyrillic lookalikes is single-script, so it needs a whole-script confusable check, which Chrome added.

blocks.md:
Arabic and Hebrew are written right to left, English left to right, and real text mixes them. Unicode stores text in **logical order** (the order you type and the order a compiler reads) and works out the **visual order** at display time, using the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm, [UAX #9](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr9/). Bidi is short for bidirectional.

The algorithm usually guesses well, but authors can steer it with invisible **explicit formatting characters**:

- Embeddings: LRE (U+202A) and RLE (U+202B), ended by PDF (U+202C, Pop Directional Formatting).
- Overrides: LRO (U+202D) and RLO (U+202E, RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE), which "force following characters" to be treated as one direction. UAX #9 says overrides "are to be avoided wherever possible, because of security concerns".
- Isolates: LRI (U+2066), RLI (U+2067), FSI (U+2068), ended by PDI (U+2069). They were added in Unicode 6.3; text inside an isolate does not affect the order of text outside it.

blocks.title: Logical order versus what the screen shows

scenes.caption: Logical order, as stored and as a compiler reads it: a, b, c, then RLO, then d, e, f, then PDF. The two controls are invisible on screen.
Display: RLO forces d, e, f to run right to left until PDF, so the screen shows a b c f e d. The bytes did not change; only the picture did.
Trojan Source, simplified from the Rust advisory: logically, everything up to the second quote is one string, and the comment sits inside it.
Rendered, the same bytes look like a comparison with "user" followed by a harmless comment. Reviewers approve the picture; the compiler builds the logic.

blocks.md:
**Case: Trojan Source, November 2021.** Nicholas Boucher and Ross Anderson of the University of Cambridge published [Trojan Source: Invisible Vulnerabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00169) (arXiv, 30 October 2021; later at USENIX Security 2023). Their abstract: source code "maliciously encoded so that it appears different to a compiler and to the human eye", with working examples in twelve languages, from C and Python to SQL, Bash and Solidity. The project site lists three techniques: **early returns** (a `return` that looks like it is inside a comment), **commenting-out** (code that looks live but is inside a comment) and **stretched strings** (code that looks live but is inside a string literal). The bidi attack is CVE-2021-42574; the homoglyph variant from lesson 9 is CVE-2021-42694.

NVD's entry carries a note from the Unicode Consortium framing it as "an issue ... in the nature of international text" affecting applications that display it, not a flaw in the algorithm. Both views lead to the same fix: tools must stop showing code in an order the compiler does not use.

The [Rust security advisory](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2021/11/01/cve-2021-42574/) shows the example in the figure, with each control written as `{U+NNNN}`:

`if access_level != "user{U+202E} {U+2066}// Check if admin{U+2069} {U+2066}" {`

which bidi-aware tools display as `if access_level != "user" { // Check if admin`. Rust received the report on 25 July 2021, scanned every crate on crates.io as of 17 October (only 5 contained these code points, none maliciously), and released Rust 1.56.1 on 1 November 2021 with two new lints, denied by default, that detect these code points in string literals and in comments; for other files it recommends checking the nine code points U+202A to U+202E and U+2066 to U+2069. GitHub began warning about files containing bidirectional Unicode text on 31 October 2021, per its [changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2021-10-31-warning-about-bidirectional-unicode-text/). GCC's (GNU Compiler Collection) [`-Wbidi-chars`](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Warning-Options.html) defaults to `unpaired`, flagging "improperly terminated bidi contexts".

blocks.title: Trojan Source coordinated disclosure, 2021 (days after 25 July)

scenes.caption: 25 July: the Cambridge researchers' report reaches the Rust Security Response WG, which starts on a fix.
14 September (day 51): Rust is told the embargo will lift on 1 November.
17 October (day 84): Rust scans all crates.io source; 5 crates contain the code points, none maliciously.
30 October to 1 November (days 97 to 99): paper on arXiv, GitHub warning live, CVE published and Rust 1.56.1 released.

blocks.md: Bidi controls are not the only invisible trick. [UTS #55](https://www.unicode.org/reports/tr55/), Unicode Source Code Handling, describes **line break spoofing**: if a C comment line ends with U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR, an editor that follows the Unicode line breaking rules shows two lines, but a compiler that does not treat U+2028 as a line end sees one long comment, so the visible null check on the "next line" is really commented out. UTS #55's remedy is for languages and editors to agree on line terminators: a language should recognise every Unicode line break, or forbid the ones it does not recognise, even inside comments. A CI (continuous integration) check catches all of these cheaply:

blocks.caption: Run on a folder containing the Rust advisory's line, it prints four findings (U+202E at column 25, U+2066 at 27, U+2069 at 45, U+2066 at 47) and exits with status 1, which fails the build. Legitimate uses can be rewritten as escapes such as `\u{202E}`.

blocks.md: Reviewers approve what they see; compilers build what is stored. Any character that changes one without the other (bidi controls, unusual line separators, lookalike identifiers) should fail the build unless it is written as a visible escape.

**Defender view.** Prevent: upgrade compilers and keep their bidi lints on (Rust 1.56.1 and later deny them; GCC warns on unpaired ones by default, and `-Wbidi-chars=any` flags every use); add the scanner above to CI for every language in the repository; configure editors to show control characters. Detect: GitHub's warning banner on a pull request is a reason to stop and inspect; scan dependency source, not only your own. Respond: if a suspicious commit is found, view it as escaped code points, revert, and review what else the same contributor touched, since this is a deliberate act, not a typo.

blocks.question: A diff renders as `if (role != "user") { // admins only`. Your scanner reports U+202E and U+2066 on that line. What should you conclude?
options: Nothing; bidi characters only affect Arabic and Hebrew text
The stored token order may differ from the displayed one, so view the line with escaped code points before approving
The compiler will reject the line automatically in every language
The line is safe because it contains a comment
blocks.explain: Overrides and isolates in code change only the display. Until you see the logical order (escaped code points, or a tool that renders by lexical structure), you do not know what the compiler will build. Only some toolchains reject these characters by default.

blocks.question: Which statement about directional isolates (U+2066 to U+2069) is correct according to UAX #9?
options: Text inside an isolate does not affect the ordering of text outside it, and vice versa
They were part of Unicode 1.0
They are always ignored by renderers
They are safe to allow anywhere in source code
blocks.explain: UAX #9 introduced isolates in Unicode 6.3 because embeddings affected their surroundings too strongly. They are still invisible reordering controls, so Rust's lints reject them in comments and literals along with embeddings and overrides.

lessons.title: URL parser differentials: one URL, two hosts

blocks.md:
A URL looks simple: `scheme://userinfo@host:port/path?query#fragment`. You met its parts in The browser security model, where scheme, host and port make an origin. The trouble is that there are two rulebooks. [RFC 3986](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986.txt) is the IETF's generic URI syntax. The WHATWG [URL Standard](https://url.spec.whatwg.org/) describes what browsers actually do. Most language libraries follow neither exactly, and Python's own documentation says `urlsplit` and `urlparse` "cannot be claimed compliant with either".

Orange Tsai's Black Hat USA 2017 talk, *A New Era of SSRF* (its slides are not linked here because they include working exploit chains), summed up the problem in one line: "It's all about the inconsistency between URL parser and requester". SSRF (server-side request forgery) means making a server send a request to a place of the attacker's choosing; the talk showed that a URL checked by one library and fetched by another could reach a different host than the one checked.

Points where parsers commonly disagree, all from the specifications:

- **Backslash.** For special schemes such as `http` and `https`, the URL Standard treats `\` like `/` (it records an "invalid-reverse-solidus" validation error and carries on). Many other parsers treat it as an ordinary character.
- **Where the authority ends.** RFC 3986 says the authority (userinfo, host, port) ends at the next `/`, `?` or `#`. The talk showed libraries that disagreed, for instance about a `#` or an extra `@` before the host.
- **Whitespace and controls.** The URL Standard strips leading and trailing C0 controls and spaces and removes tabs and newlines anywhere. Python adopted tab and newline removal in 3.10 and leading-only C0 stripping in 3.12, after [CVE-2022-0391](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-0391) and [CVE-2023-24329](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-24329), where a URL starting with blank characters could "bypass blocklisting methods".
- **Unicode.** NFKC and IDNA processing (lessons 5 and 10) can turn non-ASCII characters into delimiters or into other hosts.

blocks.code:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

def redirect_ok_bad(url):                      # suffix check on Python's view
    host = urlsplit(url).hostname or ""
    return host.endswith("good.example")

def redirect_ok_good(url):
    if any(c in url for c in "\\\t\r\n") or url != url.strip():
        return False                           # refuse what parsers disagree on
    u = urlsplit(url)
    return (u.scheme == "https" and u.hostname == "good.example"
            and u.username is None and u.port is None)

for url in ["https://good.example/home",
            "https://evil.example\\good.example/",
            "https://evilgood.example/"]:
    print(f"{url:38} python_host={urlsplit(url).hostname!s:28} "
          f"bad={redirect_ok_bad(url)!s:5} good={redirect_ok_good(url)}")
blocks.caption: Output: the first URL passes both. For the backslash URL, Python's host is the whole string `evil.example\good.example`, and for `evilgood.example` the suffix check also says yes: `bad=True good=False` for both. Node's WHATWG `URL` gives hosts `good.example`, `evil.example`, `evilgood.example`.

blocks.title: The checker and the browser read different hosts

next URL with a backslash
before good.example

scenes.caption: A login page takes a `next` URL to redirect to after sign-in. The server checks it in Python before redirecting.
Python's urlsplit treats the backslash as an ordinary character, so the host is `evil.example\good.example`.

scenes.caption: The suffix check `endswith("good.example")` is true, so the server sends the redirect. Two mistakes here: a suffix test, and a different parser from the browser's.

scenes.caption: The browser parses with the URL Standard: backslash acts as a slash, so the host is `evil.example` and the rest is path.

labels.py:
