scenes.caption: The fix: refuse characters the parsers disagree on, require an exact host match, and where possible parse with the same rules the browser uses.

labels.py:
Parse once, exact host,
refuse ambiguity

blocks.md:
The talk also showed a Unicode case in Node.js: a check refused `..` in a path, yet U+FF2E FULLWIDTH LATIN CAPITAL LETTER N (bytes FF 2E) reached the server as a dot, because the HTTP module of the time lost the high byte and kept only 0x2E. In Python terms, `bytes(ord(c) & 0xFF for c in "ＮＮ")` is `b'..'`, while `".." in "ＮＮ"` is `False`. Lossy conversion again, as in lesson 8. Current Node.js refuses such request paths with an `ERR_UNESCAPED_CHARACTERS` error; the general fix is to percent-encode non-ASCII characters before sending, never to truncate them.

The talk's application-level mitigation is short: "Use the only IP and hostname, do not reuse the input URL". In other words, parse once, validate the parsed host, then build the outgoing request from those parsed parts rather than handing the original string to a second parser.

A suffix check like `host.endswith("good.example")` is wrong even with a perfect parser: `evilgood.example` passes it. Compare the whole host exactly, or check for a dot boundary (`host == d or host.endswith("." + d)`).

**Defender view.** Prevent: one parser per decision, the same rules as the consumer (for browser redirects, prefer relative paths you build yourself, or a WHATWG-compliant parser); exact host allowlists; refuse backslashes, control characters, userinfo and unexpected ports; for server-side fetches, resolve the name, check the IP address, and connect to that address (the full SSRF defence is in Server-side attacks, "Validating outbound URLs in code"). Detect: log the raw `next` or URL parameter and the parsed host side by side; alert when they differ in unusual ways (backslashes, `@`, encoded characters in the host). Respond: find redirects or fetches that left your domains, review sessions or tokens that may have leaked, and fix the parser use, not just the one input.

blocks.question: Your redirect check uses Python's `urlsplit` and an exact host match; the browser follows the URL. Which input class is still most likely to cause a disagreement?
options: A plain `https://good.example/path`
URLs with a query string
URLs containing backslashes or control characters, which the URL Standard handles differently from many libraries
Upper-case scheme names like `HTTPS`
blocks.explain: Backslashes and control characters are exactly where WHATWG repair rules and other libraries diverge. Ordinary paths, queries and scheme case are handled the same by both.

blocks.question: What is the core of Orange Tsai's application-level mitigation for SSRF parser differentials?
options: Use a longer blocklist of internal IP ranges
Parse the URL once, validate the parsed host or IP, and build the request from those parts instead of reusing the raw input
Percent-decode the URL twice before checking
Only allow URLs shorter than 100 characters
blocks.explain: If the component that fetches never re-parses the original string, there is no second interpretation to disagree with. Blocklists and length limits do not address the differential.

lessons.title: JSON differentials: duplicate keys, numbers and CouchDB

blocks.md:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) looks too simple to argue about, but its standard leaves two important things open. [RFC 8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259.txt) says "the names within an object SHOULD be unique", and that when they are not, "the behavior of software that receives such an object is unpredictable. Many implementations report the last name/value pair only. Other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some implementations report all of the name/value pairs". For numbers, it says only integers in the range from $-(2^{53})+1$ to $2^{53}-1$ are interoperable, meaning implementations "will agree exactly on their numeric values".

So `{"roles": ["admin"], "roles": []}` is legal JSON whose meaning depends on who reads it.

blocks.caption: Output: `validator sees: []` / `store uses:     ['admin']` / `strict parser: duplicate keys: ['roles']` / `9007199254740993`. In Node, `JSON.parse` of the same number gives `9007199254740992`, and of a duplicate key keeps the last value.

blocks.md:
**Case: Apache CouchDB, November 2017.** CouchDB is a database whose user accounts are documents in a special `_users` database. Before a write is accepted, a JavaScript validation function checks it, for example that you are not giving yourself the `_admin` role. Max Justicz, a security researcher, found that the JavaScript parser and jiffy, the parser on CouchDB's Erlang side (Erlang: the language CouchDB is written in), disagreed on duplicate keys: JavaScript kept the last value, jiffy kept both, and CouchDB's internal lookup returned the first. A sign-up document with two `roles` keys, first `_admin` and last empty, passed validation and created an administrator.

[CVE-2017-12635](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2017-12635) records it for CouchDB before 1.7.0 and 2.x before 2.1.1; with CVE-2017-12636 it led to shell access. The [CouchDB advisory](https://blog.couchdb.org/2017/11/14/apache-couchdb-cve-2017-12635-and-cve-2017-12636/) says the fix made the Erlang side keep the last key too. Justicz's guess that the npm registry was exposed was later corrected: it was not.

blocks.title: One document, two parsers, two answers

scenes.caption: A sign-up document with the key `roles` twice: first `["_admin"]`, then `[]`.
The JavaScript validator keeps the last value, sees an empty role list, and approves the write.
The Erlang side keeps both pairs and its lookup returns the first: `_admin`. That copy is what is stored and used.
Authorisation for later requests reads the stored document through the Erlang side. The new user is an administrator.
The fix makes the parsers agree (CouchDB 1.7.0 and 2.1.1). The general fix is to reject duplicates at the edge, so no reader ever sees an ambiguous document.

blocks.md: Jake Miller of Bishop Fox, a security consultancy, [surveyed 49 JSON parsers](https://bishopfox.com/blog/json-interoperability-vulnerabilities) in February 2021 and grouped the interoperability risks into categories including inconsistent duplicate-key precedence, key collisions through character truncation and comments, and inconsistent float and integer representation. One example: a parser that decodes too-large numbers as 0 can make a payment step and a cart step disagree about a quantity. Justicz's own conclusion fits all of them: "It's probably a bad idea to use more than one parser to process the same data."

blocks.title: Gap between neighbouring doubles: integers stop being exact after 2^53

scenes.caption: JavaScript stores every number as a 64-bit IEEE 754 double (the IEEE floating-point standard) with 53 bits of precision. Below 2^53 the gap between neighbouring values is at most 1, so every integer is exact.
Where the gap curve crosses the integer-step line, at 2^53 (about 9.007 x 10^15), the gap becomes 2: 9007199254740993 rounds to 9007199254740992, as Node showed. Python's int keeps it exact.

blocks.md: Reject duplicate keys and out-of-range numbers at the first parser, then pass the parsed (or re-serialised, canonical) object onward. Never forward the original bytes to a second parser and assume it reads them the same way.

**Defender view.** Prevent: a strict parse at the edge (`object_pairs_hook` that raises on duplicates in Python; schema validation that forbids unknown and repeated fields), numbers that must be exact sent as strings or kept in the interoperable range, and one parser per decision. Detect: count and log documents rejected for duplicate keys; in a mature API they should be nearly zero, so a spike is probing. Respond: search stored records for duplicate keys or values that differ between your services' views, and check privileges granted through any affected path.

blocks.question: Two services read the same JSON body. Service A keeps the first value of a duplicate key, service B the last. Which design removes the disagreement?
options: Reject documents with duplicate keys at the entry point, then forward the parsed object or a canonical re-serialisation
Tell clients not to send duplicates
Make both services keep the first value, by convention
Sort the keys alphabetically
blocks.explain: Asking clients to behave does nothing against an attacker. Aligning two parsers by convention breaks again when a library changes. Rejecting at the edge and forwarding only unambiguous data means there is nothing to disagree about.

blocks.question: A Go service decodes a quantity as a float64 and a Python service as an int. For which quantity can they first disagree?
blocks.explain: Doubles represent every integer up to 2^53 = 9007199254740992 exactly. 9007199254740993 is the first integer that rounds (to ...992). The other values are exact in both.

lessons.title: XML, multipart forms and email addresses: same bytes, different trees

blocks.md:
The pattern from JSON repeats in every structured format: whenever two components parse the same bytes, ask what each one returns for the awkward cases. Three formats matter constantly in web security.

**XML and SAML.** SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) single sign-on sends a signed XML document saying who a user is. The course SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML teaches the signature checks and the classic attack, in "XML signature wrapping: the verifier and the app read different parts". That course also walks through the 2024 ruby-saml bug (CVE-2024-45409); here we add its parser-level sequel.

**Case: ruby-saml, March 2025.** GitHub Security Lab's Peter Stöckli [described](https://github.blog/security/sign-in-as-anyone-bypassing-saml-sso-authentication-with-parser-differentials/) the finding: Stöckli and a bug bounty participant known as ahacker1 each noticed during review that ruby-saml read the same SAML response with two different XML parsers: REXML (pure Ruby) and Nokogiri (which wraps libxml2). The signature value and the expected digest were extracted with REXML; the signed element and the SignedInfo block that was verified were extracted and canonicalised with Nokogiri. If the two parsers could be made to see different `Signature` elements, the library would verify one and trust another. [CVE-2025-25291](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-25291) states that "ReXML and Nokogiri parse XML differently; the parsers can generate entirely different document structures from the same XML input", allowing signature wrapping and authentication bypass. Fixed versions 1.12.4 and 1.18.0 shipped on 12 March 2025; GitLab coordinated a release of its own product.

blocks.title: ruby-saml: one response, two XML parsers

scenes.caption: One SAML response arrives. ruby-saml hands it to two parsers in the same verification function.
REXML supplies the SignatureValue and the DigestValue that the signed content must match.
Nokogiri supplies the SignedInfo that is verified and the assertion that is hashed.
If a crafted document makes the two parsers see different Signature elements, the checks compare pieces of two different signatures and can pass for unsigned content.
The patch ties hash and signature checks back together; the blog notes removing one parser was planned for a later major release.

blocks.md: **Multipart forms.** File uploads and many forms use `multipart/form-data` ([RFC 7578](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7578.txt)): the body is split into parts by a boundary string, and each part has a `Content-Disposition` header with a `name` and optionally a `filename`. Repeated names are legal (RFC 7578 has a section on multiple files for one field), so two parsers in a chain, such as a fraud check and a payment handler, can legitimately pick different occurrences. The RFC also tells receivers not to use a supplied file name blindly and to ignore any directory path in it.

blocks.caption: Output: `10 10000` / `duplicate field amount`. Toy parsers on a tiny body; real ones also differ on quoting, encodings and boundaries.

blocks.md: **Email addresses.** An address header can carry a display name, comments and angle brackets, and [RFC 5322](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5322.txt)'s grammar is subtle. [CVE-2023-27043](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-27043) found that Python's `email.utils.parseaddr` and `getaddresses` could return the wrong part of a malformed header as the address. NVD's example is a sign-up that grants access only after verifying receipt of email at a `@company.example.com` address; the issue report explains how the check can read one address while the reply goes to another. The [cpython issue](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/102988) notes that Go's parser returned an error for the same inputs. Python 3.13 added a `strict` parameter and made it the default, and the change was backported to security releases of older branches (3.12.6, for example), so malformed input now returns `('', '')`.

blocks.code:
import re
from email.utils import parseaddr

header = "alice@corp.example <bob@evil.example>"     # malformed To: value

def lenient_check(h):            # old default (before 3.13 / 3.12.6)
    return parseaddr(h, strict=False)[1]

def angle_first(h):              # toy mailer: prefers the address in <...>
    m = re.search(r"<([^>]*)>", h)
    return m.group(1) if m else h

def strict_check(h):             # default since 3.13 / 3.12.6
    name, addr = parseaddr(h)
    if not addr:
        raise ValueError("malformed address header")
    return addr

print("allow-list sees:", lenient_check(header))
print("mail goes to:   ", angle_first(header))
try:
    strict_check(header)
except ValueError as e:
    print("strict:", e)
blocks.caption: Output: `allow-list sees: alice@corp.example` / `mail goes to:    bob@evil.example` / `strict: malformed address header`. This header is malformed in a similar way to the report's cases, not one of its exact inputs; `angle_first` is a toy.

blocks.md: For every structured format: one strict parser at the boundary, reject anything ambiguous (duplicate fields, malformed headers, unknown XML structure), and pass the parsed result, not the original bytes, to the rest of the system.

**Defender view.** Prevent: upgrade SAML libraries promptly and prefer ones that parse once; reject multipart bodies with duplicate single-value fields and generate stored file names yourself; use strict address parsing and verify ownership by sending to the parsed address and requiring a click. Detect: GitHub's post suggests looking for SAML logins from IP addresses that do not fit the user's usual location, since no reliable exploit indicator exists; log parse rejections per endpoint. Respond: for SAML, review recent logins through the affected library and force re-authentication; for sign-up checks, re-verify accounts created through the lenient path.

blocks.question: Why did using two XML parsers in one verification function make ruby-saml exploitable?
options: XML parsers are always slower than JSON parsers
REXML cannot parse signatures
The signature and the digest checks could be fed from different elements if the parsers built different trees from the same input
Nokogiri ignores XML namespaces
blocks.explain: Each check was correct in isolation, but they used values extracted by different parsers. A document the two parsers read differently lets each check approve a different thing.

blocks.question: A fraud service reads the first `amount` field of a multipart body and the payment service reads the last. What is the right fix?
options: Reject requests where a single-value field appears more than once, at the first parser, and forward the parsed values
Make the fraud service read the last value too
Limit the body size
Encode amounts in base64
blocks.explain: Aligning the two services by convention works until one library changes. Rejecting the ambiguity at the edge means both services receive one unambiguous value.

lessons.title: Polyglot files, content sniffing and LangSec

blocks.md:
A **polyglot** is, in the definition of Jonas Magazinius, Billy K. Rios and Andrei Sabelfeld's 2013 paper [Polyglots: Crossing Origins by Crossing Formats](https://www.cse.chalmers.se/~andrei/ccs13.pdf), "a program that is valid in multiple programming languages"; in practice, a file that is valid in two or more formats at once. Their abstract calls polyglots "the root cause of a large class of attacks" that "exploit the mismatch between the expected and provided content", singles out PDF as a particularly dangerous format, and reports content-smuggling problems at two major cloud storage services.

Polyglots work because formats are read from different places. Many check a **magic number**, a fixed signature in the first bytes (`GIF89a` for GIF images). A ZIP reader works differently: the [ZIP specification](https://pkware.cachefly.net/webdocs/casestudies/APPNOTE.TXT) puts the "end of central directory record" last, and readers find the archive's index there, so data in front does not matter.

blocks.code:
import io, zipfile

buf = io.BytesIO()
with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w") as z:
    z.writestr("note.txt", "hello from inside the zip")
blob = b"GIF89a" + b"\x00" * 10 + buf.getvalue()     # image magic, then a zip

def sniff(data):                                      # a typical upload check
    return "image/gif" if data.startswith(b"GIF89a") else "unknown"

print(sniff(blob))
with zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(blob)) as z:          # zip readers start at the end
    print(z.namelist(), z.read("note.txt"))
blocks.caption: Output: `image/gif` / `['note.txt'] b'hello from inside the zip'`. Python's zipfile docs note that appending a ZIP to another file, such as an executable, is a supported use.

blocks.title: One file, two readers starting at opposite ends

scenes.caption: The bytes of the file, in order: a GIF signature, some filler, then a complete ZIP archive whose index sits at the very end.
The upload check reads the first six bytes, sees GIF89a, and labels the file an image.
A ZIP reader starts at the end, finds the end-of-central-directory record, then follows offsets back to the file entries. The GIF bytes are never looked at.
Both readers are correct by their own rules. The flaw is a system that checks with one and later hands the file to the other.

blocks.md:
Browsers add a third reader: **content sniffing**, where a browser guesses a type from the bytes instead of trusting the `Content-Type` header. The WHATWG [MIME Sniffing Standard](https://mimesniff.spec.whatwg.org/) defines those rules (MIME: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, type labels such as `image/gif`). Serving user uploads with an accurate `Content-Type`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and from a separate origin keeps a polyglot from being reinterpreted in your site's origin.

**LangSec** (language-theoretic security) is the research view that ties this course together. In the 2011 ;login: article [The Halting Problems of Network Stack Insecurity](https://www.usenix.org/publications/login/december-2011-volume-36-number-6/halting-problems-network-stack-insecurity), Len Sassaman, Meredith L. Patterson, Sergey Bratus and Anna Shubina argue that code handling input acts as a **recognizer** for an input language, and that exploitation is often a recognizer bug. They cite earlier work on X.509 certificates, where different parsers handled multiple Common Names differently.

Three LangSec ideas you can apply directly:

1. **Recognise the whole input first.** Treat input handling as a recognizer: decide whether the entire input is valid against a precise grammar before acting on any part of it, instead of checking pieces as you go. The [LangSec site](https://langsec.org/) warns that for complex input languages "full recognition of valid or expected inputs may be UNDECIDABLE", which is the argument for simple formats.
2. **Keep input languages simple.** The authors argue that checking two implementations agree is undecidable for sufficiently complex input languages, so they recommend keeping message formats to "a necessary minimum of computational power required for their recognition".

**3. Rethink Postel's law.** Jon Postel's robustness principle, from the TCP specification (RFC 793), "be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others", maximises interoperability "at the unfortunate expense of consistent parser behavior, and thus at the expense of security". The IETF's Internet Architecture Board revisited the principle in [RFC 9413](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9413.txt), Maintaining Robust Protocols (2023), observing that some interpretations of it harm interoperability over time.

Every fix in this course is one of these: strict decoders (1), canonical forms and allowlists (2), and rejecting rather than repairing malformed input (3).

Checking the first bytes of an upload is not validation. A file can carry one format's signature and another format's content. If a file must be an image, decode it with an image library and re-encode it to a fresh file; whatever was hidden in it does not survive.

**Defender view.** Prevent: re-encode images and documents on upload where you can; store uploads outside the web root with server-generated names; serve them from a separate domain with correct `Content-Type`, `nosniff` and `Content-Disposition: attachment` for anything not meant to render (file upload handling in full: Server-side attacks, "File uploads: names, types, storage and execution"). Detect: files whose detected type differs by reader (run more than one identifier on uploads and alert on disagreement); archives with leading data. Respond: remove the file, check who downloaded or rendered it, and look for similar uploads from the same account.

blocks.question: An upload filter accepts files that start with `GIF89a`. Why can a ZIP archive still get through and be opened as a ZIP later?
options: ZIP files always start with GIF89a
ZIP readers locate the archive from the end-of-central-directory record at the end, so leading bytes are ignored
The filter decompresses the file first
GIF and ZIP use the same compression
blocks.explain: The GIF check reads the start; the ZIP reader starts from the end. Both are right about their own format, and a file can satisfy both.

blocks.question: Which practice best follows the LangSec idea of recognising the whole input before acting on it?
options: Process each field as soon as it is read, to save memory
Accept malformed input and repair it, as Postel's law suggests
Use regular expressions to block known-bad substrings
Parse and validate the entire input against a strict grammar, and only then act on it
blocks.explain: Acting on partial input means the system may have done something before it discovers the input was invalid. Repairing input and blocklisting substrings both widen the accepted language instead of fixing it.

lessons.title: Defender's checklist for encodings and parsers, and where to practise

blocks.md:
Every lesson in this course came back to the same two root causes: a check that runs before a transformation, and two parsers reading one input. The checklist below turns them into habits for code review and design review. For each input that crosses a trust boundary, ask:

1. **Where is it decoded, and how many times?** Exactly once per layer, strictly (no overlongs, no junk base64, no repairing).
2. **Where is it normalised and case-folded?** Before validation, with NFKC plus case folding for identifiers, and with an idempotence check.
3. **What lossy conversions happen later?** Code pages, byte truncation, IDNA mapping. Check the converted value, or remove the conversion.
4. **How many parsers read it?** If more than one, reject ambiguity at the first and forward the parsed result.
5. **What does a human see?** Confusables and bidi controls create a third reader, the reviewer or user.

blocks.title: Where each control belongs in a request path

scenes.caption: A request enters at the edge and passes through decoding, the application's own parsing, and finally the action (database, filesystem, outbound request, email).
Edge and decoding: one strict decode per layer; reject invalid UTF-8, non-canonical base64 and leftover escapes. Log raw and decoded forms.
Normalisation: NFKC + casefold for identifiers, idempotence checked, skeleton collisions refused. Validation happens after this box, never before.
Parsing: one strict parser per format; duplicates and malformed structure rejected; the parsed object, not the raw bytes, is passed on.
Action: allowlists on the final value (exact host, resolved path, stored email address); outbound requests built from parsed parts; deny by default.

blocks.md:
**Detection signals**, collected from the lessons, for a web application's logs and a code repository:

- Requests your strict decoders reject (invalid UTF-8, bad base64, `%25` sequences in paths), grouped by client.
- Inputs that change under NFKC in security-relevant fields, and sign-ups whose canonical name or skeleton collides with an existing one.
- Password resets where the submitted address is not byte-for-byte the stored one.
- Duplicate JSON keys or duplicate single-value form fields, which a healthy client never sends.
- Redirect or fetch targets whose raw and parsed hosts differ.
- Commits or dependencies containing bidi controls or unusual line separators (the CI scanner from lesson 11).

Tools that help: [CyberChef](https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/), a browser-based "Cyber Swiss Army Knife" from GCHQ (the UK signals intelligence agency) for decoding and converting data step by step, and Burp Suite's [Decoder](https://portswigger.net/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/decoder), which shows what a value becomes under each encoding. Both show you transformations; neither tells you which one your server performs, so test against your own stack.

**Responding** to a finding follows one pattern. First, identify both readers and write down what each one returns for the input. Second, fix the design (one parser, check after the transformation, reject ambiguity), not just the single input you were shown, because attackers will find the next spelling. Third, search history: replay stored raw inputs through the fixed code to find records that were accepted under the old behaviour, such as accounts with non-canonical names, files outside allowed folders, or redirects that left your domains. Spotify's post describes exactly this step: it found the hijacked accounts by looking for stored canonical names that were wrong.

Only test systems you own or have written permission to test; the legal line is covered in Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits.

**Practise legally:**

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security): free labs on path traversal, SSRF, request smuggling and other web bugs, used with Burp Suite Community Edition.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/): a deliberately insecure web shop you run locally, for practising web bugs end to end.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/): Carnegie Mellon CyLab's learning platform, where picoCTF now points learners.
- Your own lab: the toy parsers in this course are a few lines each. Write a second parser for any format you use, feed both the same inputs, and log every disagreement. That is how many of the real cases here were found.
Two questions catch most bugs in this course: "Is this check running on the exact value that will be used?" and "Is anything else going to parse these bytes?"

blocks.question: A team fixes a reported bypass by adding the attacker's exact input to a blocklist. Why is that a weak response?
options: Blocklists are slow
Blocklists cannot hold Unicode
The underlying differential remains, so other spellings of the same meaning will still pass
It is a strong response if the list is reviewed monthly
blocks.explain: The bug is the disagreement between a check and a later reader. As long as it exists, an attacker can find another encoding, normalisation or parser quirk that produces the same effect.

blocks.question: Which pairing of bug and design fix from this course is correct?
options: Spotify takeover: switch to bcrypt password hashing
CouchDB roles: reject duplicate JSON keys before any component acts on the document
Trojan Source: normalise source files with NFKC
PHP CVE-2024-4577: add a CSP header
blocks.explain: CouchDB's bug was two parsers disagreeing on duplicate keys. Spotify needed an idempotent canonicalisation, Trojan Source needs bidi controls rejected or made visible (NFKC leaves them alone), and the PHP bug needs no lossy ANSI conversion before argument parsing.

blocks.question: You find that your login redirect check and the browser disagree on hosts for URLs containing backslashes. After fixing the code, what is the most important next step?
options: Search logs for past redirect parameters whose parsed hosts differed, and review the sessions involved
Close the ticket
Rotate the TLS certificate
Disable all redirects permanently
blocks.explain: A differential may have been used before you found it. Replaying stored raw inputs through both parsers tells you whether anyone was sent off-site, which decides the rest of the response.
